description_full: Live Nation Entertainment, Inc. operates as a live entertainment company worldwide. The company operates through Concerts, Ticketing, and Sponsorship & Advertising segments. Its Concerts segment promotes live music events in its owned or operated venues, and in rented third-party venues. This segment operates and manages music venues; produces music festivals; creates associated content; and offers management and other services to artists. The Ticketing segment manages the ticketing operations, including the provision of ticketing software and services to consumers with marketplace for tickets and event information through mobile apps, other websites, and retail outlets, as well as its websites, such as livenation.com and ticketmaster.com; and provides ticket resale services. This segment offers ticketing services for arenas, stadiums, amphitheaters, music clubs, concert promoters, professional sports franchises and leagues, college sports teams, performing arts venues, museums, and theaters. Its Sponsorship & Advertising segment sells international, national, and local sponsorships and placement of advertising, including signage, online advertising, and promotional programs; rich media offering, including advertising related with live streaming and music-related content; and ads through distribution network of venues, events, and websites. This segment also manages the development of strategic sponsorship programs, as well as develops, books, and produces custom events or programs for specific brands. It owns, operates, or leases entertainment venues. The company was formerly known as Live Nation, Inc. and changed its name to Live Nation Entertainment, Inc. in January 2010. Live Nation Entertainment, Inc. was incorporated in 2005 and is headquartered in Beverly Hills, California.

financial_summary: Live Nation Entertainment, Inc. is a large-cap communication services business with a $42.1B market cap on $25.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +15% over the past three years and +13% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 14% against a 9% cost of capital, a 4-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $334M in free cash flow — roughly 1 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.81× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.3× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 4.0×.

Shareholder yield is only 0.1%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 32% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 170% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 2 other valuation measures)
Very elevated short interest (15.9% of float) — sophisticated money is betting against the business
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Piotroski score 4/9 — below the median for a healthy business
Altman Z in the grey zone — financial health warrants monitoring
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $36.3M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Advertising-cycle exposure and content/regulatory risk — a single platform policy shift or ad-spend contraction cascades through the P&L quickly.
Cord-cutting acceleration and audience fragmentation — legacy distribution bundles unravel faster than subscription revenue can replace them.
AI-generated content commoditisation — as creation costs collapse toward zero, content libraries lose pricing power and differentiation narrows.

sect: Its 5% operating margin is roughly in line with the Communication Services median (9%).

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 25% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 6% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 29% and a beta of 1.11, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.58 vs 5y 1.14), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $313.5M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 61% in the 2020 crash, 47% in the 2022 bear market and 86% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $66.13 (margin of safety -170%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 32%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $40.15 to $108 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Communication Services peers: P/E 91.0 vs 15.4, EV/EBITDA 22.2 vs 9.9 and P/FCF 126.1 vs 11.1 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-2%).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 0.8% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 24 covering analysts target $204 on average, 14% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 14% earns above the cost of capital of 9.2%, but the 4pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 2.85).
It converts 1% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.81x.
ROE of 183% is amplified by 84.5x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
Operating margin is running 12pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 0.6% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.3x net debt to EBITDA ($7.1B of cash against $7.6B of debt), with interest covered 4.0x.
The current ratio of 1.00 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 14.7% over 3 years, 68.4% over 5 years and 13.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 75%).
At current returns, reinvesting 52% of profits supports about 7.1% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex runs 1.7x depreciation (4.2% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 69, clearing the bar for a healthy growth business.
It has missed earnings estimates by 97.8% on average.
own: Insiders own 32.4%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 86%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (5 sales, net $36.3M sold).
The share count has grown 1.5% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
Short interest is elevated at 15.9% of the float, 14.1 days to cover.
people: With about 17,700 employees, each generates about $1.4M of revenue, 2.3x the Communication Services median, and revenue has grown 11.7% a year across its filed history.

CEO pay is $22.6M (16x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
